title: Module 2: Internal actions, shear force and bending moment
shortTitle: Internal actions, shear force and bending moment
whyItMatters: External loads and support reactions only tell half the story; designing a member requires cutting it open conceptually to find internal axial force N, shear force V, and bending moment M along its entire length.
introduction: Covers the method of sections to expose internal axial force, shear force, and bending moment, standard UK structural engineering sign conventions (sagging positive, BMD plotted on the tension face), load–shear–moment differential relationships, deflected shapes, and locating tension and compression faces.
objectives: Cut a structural member at any section x and determine internal N(x), V(x), and M(x) by equilibrium.
Construct accurate Shear Force Diagrams (SFDs) and Bending Moment Diagrams (BMDs) for simply supported, cantilever, and overhanging beams.
Sketch deflected shapes, points of contraflexure, and tension/compression zones before calculating.
learningGate: Draw SFD and BMD diagrams without copying from a formula sheet.,Calculate maximum bending moment and maximum shear force accurately.,Predict the shape of the diagram and deflected curve before calculating it.,Identify tension and compression zones for sagging, hogging, and cantilever beams.,Explain why a beam may need shear checks close to supports even where bending moment is low.

topics.title: Internal Actions, Section Cuts & Sign Conventions
topics.summary: Covers cutting a member to reveal internal axial force N, shear force V, and bending moment M, positive sagging vs negative hogging conventions, and checking equilibrium of left and right free-body segments.
subtopics: Method of sections: cutting a member to expose internal N, V, and M
Physical meaning of axial tension (+N), axial compression (-N), shear V, and bending moment M

UK structural convention: plotting the BMD on the tension face of the member
Consistency check: evaluating internal M(x) from the left segment vs the right segment

questions.learningObjective: Identify tension and compression faces in sagging vs hogging
questions.prompt: When a horizontal beam undergoes positive (sagging) bending, which extreme fibres are in tension and which are in compression?
questions.assumptions: Under hogging (over an internal support or in a gravity-loaded cantilever), the top fibres are in tension and the bottom fibres are in compression.
options: Bottom fibres are in tension and top fibres are in compression
Top fibres are in tension and bottom fibres are in.
By assuming a uniform linear-elastic stress dist.
Stresses are uniform compression across the entire depth
questions.explanation: Sagging curves the beam concave upwards (like a smile), stretching the bottom fibres in tension and shortening the top fibres in compression. Engineering synthesis for "Identify tension and compression faces in sagging vs hogging": always trace the complete load path from point of application to the foundations, ensure compatibility between analysis boundary assumptions and physical site detailing, and verify against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 2 (Internal Actions: Axial, Shear & Bending Diagrams).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate internal shear force at a section cut (Example 2.1)
questions.prompt: A 6.0 m simply supported beam carries a UDL of w = 10 kN/m (left reaction R_A = 30 kN). Cut the beam at x = 1.5 m from the left support A. What is the internal shear force V at x = 1.5 m?
questions.explanation: From the left free body of length 1.5 m: V(1.5) = R_A − w × x = 30 − (10 × 1.5) = 15 kN. questions.learningObjective: Calculate internal bending moment at a section cut (Example 2.1)
questions.prompt: A 6.0 m simply supported beam carries a uniform distributed load of w = 10 kN/m over its full span (so the left support reaction is R_A = 30 kN). Calculate the internal sagging bending moment M at a section x = 1.5 m from the left support.
questions.assumptions: Remember the UDL over the 1.5 m segment (15 kN) acts at its centroid 0.75 m from the cut.
questions.explanation: From the left free body: M(1.5) = R_A × 1.5 − (10 × 1.5) × (1.5 / 2) = 45.0 − 11.25 = 33.75 kN·m. questions.learningObjective: Understand UK convention for plotting Bending Moment Diagrams
questions.prompt: In UK structural engineering practice (Eurocode / IStructE convention), on which side of the member axis is the Bending Moment Diagram plotted, and why?
questions.assumptions: Always state your sign/plotting convention on calculation sheets.
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel
On the tension face (bottom for sagging, top for hogging), so it immediately shows where tensile reinforcement in concrete or lateral restraint of the opposite compression flange in steel is needed

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
questions.explanation: Plotting the BMD on the tension side directly visualises where main tension reinforcement is required in RC beams and reminds steel designers which flange is the opposite compression flange.
questions.citation: Euler-Bernoulli Beam Theory & UK Sagging/Hogging Sign Convention

questions.learningObjective: Verify equilibrium consistency between left-hand and right-hand free bodies
questions.prompt: If you cut a beam in equilibrium at section x and calculate internal bending moment M(x) using the left-hand free body, and then recalculate M(x) independently using the right-hand free body, how must the two results compare?
questions.assumptions: Evaluating M(x) from the shorter side of the cut is a fast hand-calculation check.
options: It redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface

It increases the elastic Euler critical buckling load by halving the effective buckling length between inflection points, provided that the connection detail transfers full axial thrust without slip or local web crippling
They must have the exact same magnitude and the same sagging/hogging sense (equal and opposite internal action-reaction pair at the cut)

It eliminates vertical shear deformation across the web depth by forcing the neutral axis to remain coincident with the geometric centroid of the uncracked transformed section throughout both construction and permanent service stages
questions.explanation: By Newton’s third law and static equilibrium, the internal moment exposed on the left face of the cut and the right face of the cut must match identically.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate maximum bending moment for simply supported UDL (Example 2.1)

questions.learningObjective: Calculate maximum bending moment under eccentric point load (Example 2.3)
questions.prompt: A 5.0 m simply supported beam carries a single 20 kN point load at x = 2.0 m from the left support (giving support reactions R_A = 12 kN and R_B = 8 kN). Calculate the maximum bending moment M_max under the point load.
questions.explanation: Shear steps from +12 kN to -8 kN at x = 2.0 m. Thus M_max occurs at x = 2.0 m and equals R_A × 2.0 m = 12 kN × 2.0 m = 24.0 kN·m (checked from right: 8 kN × 3.0 m = 24.0 kN·m).

questions.learningObjective: Relate load type to SFD and BMD curve degree
questions.prompt: Over a beam span loaded by a constant downward UDL (w = constant), what are the mathematical shapes of the Shear Force Diagram (SFD) and Bending Moment Diagram (BMD)?
questions.assumptions: Under point loads only (w = 0 between loads), the SFD is piecewise constant (rectangular steps) and the BMD is piecewise linear (triangular).
options: The member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces

The structural analysis models the joint as a frictionless pin for vertical gravity load takedown but simultaneously assumes full rotational fixity when evaluating lateral storey drift and global second-order sway stability

The design substitutes the characteristic 95th-percentile material strength in place of the 5th-percentile characteristic strength and omits the combination factor ψ_0 when superimpose-combining independent variable wind and imposed floor actions
The SFD is a sloping straight line (linear) and the BMD is a curve of second degree (parabola)
questions.explanation: Integrating a constant w once gives a linear shear function V(x) = V₀ − wx; integrating a second time gives a quadratic (parabolic) moment function M(x).

questions.learningObjective: Enforce boundary conditions on a cantilever deflected shape
questions.prompt: When sketching the deflected shape of a horizontal cantilever fixed into a rigid wall at the left end A and loaded downward at the right tip B, what must be true of the curve at A?
questions.assumptions: Violating zero slope at a fixed support is one of the most common sketching mistakes.
options: Both the vertical displacement and the slope (rotation tangent) must be zero at the fixed wall A, curving smoothly downward to the right (hogging)
The beam starts at A with an immediate downward kink (non-zero slope) like a pin support, assuming that by applying the unfactored char.
The vertical displacement is maximum at A and zero at B
By taking the mean 50th-percentile material stiffness modulus together with a fully fixed rotational boundary condition at both e.
questions.explanation: A fixed support prevents both translation (y(0) = 0) and rotation (dy/dx(0) = 0), so the deflected curve must emerge horizontally from the wall before curving downward.

questions.learningObjective: Define a point of contraflexure on a beam
questions.prompt: What occurs physically and mathematically at a point of contraflexure along a beam?
questions.assumptions: Notice that deflection is generally NOT zero at a point of contraflexure.
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel
The bending moment M(x) passes through zero and changes sign (from sagging to hogging or vice versa), so the curvature of the deflected shape reverses

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
questions.explanation: Since curvature κ = M/(EI), where M = 0 the curvature is zero and transitions between concave-up (sagging) and concave-down (hogging). Engineering synthesis for "Define a point of contraflexure on a beam": always trace the complete load path from point of application to the foundations, ensure compatibility between analysis boundary assumptions and physical site detailing, and verify against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 2 (Internal Actions: Axial, Shear & Bending Diagrams).

questions.learningObjective: Explain why shear checks are required near supports where moment is low (Module 2 Gate)
questions.prompt: At the pin or roller end support of a simply supported beam, the bending moment M is zero. Why must the engineer still check the beam closely at and near the support?
options: Because bending stress σ = M/Z becomes infinite when M = 0

It increases the elastic Euler critical buckling load by halving the effective buckling length between inflection points, provided that the connection detail transfers full axial thrust without slip or local web crippling
Because the shear force V is typically at its maximum at the supports, and heavy point loads located close to a support produce very large shear forces while generating only a small bending moment
Because lateral torsional buckling only occurs where M = 0
questions.explanation: Shear force V and web bearing are greatest at the supports. In short-span transfer beams or where a column/needle lands close to a support, shear failure of the web or bearing failure governs well before midspan bending.

questions.learningObjective: Locate where shear passes through zero under asymmetric loading
questions.prompt: A 6.0 m simply supported beam carries a full-span UDL of w = 10 kN/m plus a downward point load outside the span on a right-hand overhang such that the left support reaction at A is R_A = 22 kN. At what distance x from the left support A does the shear force V(x) pass through zero (where peak sagging moment occurs)?
questions.assumptions: Peak sagging moment in the span occurs at x = 2.2 m, not at midspan (3.0 m).
questions.explanation: In span AB: V(x) = R_A − w·x = 22 − 10x. Setting V(x) = 0 gives x = 22 / 10 = 2.2 m. Step-by-step verification for "Locate where shear passes through zero under asymmetric loading": confirm that all input quantities are converted into consistent SI metric units before substitution, evaluate the governing equilibrium or constitutive equation to obtain 2.2 m, and cross-check the magnitude and sign against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 2 (Internal Actions: Axial, Shear & Bending Diagrams).
